newsitem.title: FRANCE: Thomson-CSF privatisation nears key phase.
newsitem.headline: Thomson-CSF privatisation nears key phase.

text.p: The privatisation of electronics group Thomson-CSF, which will be decisive for the future of the French defence industry and has far-reaching European consequences, is nearing the final lap.

The Le Monde newspaper said on Tuesday the government's "cahier des charges" -- a detailed legal and financial document setting out conditions for selling the state's stake in a private placement -- could be published as early as Friday.
A Finance Ministry spokeswoman declined comment on the timing.

The supervisory board of Thomson-CSF, 58 percent owned by state company Thomson SA, was meeting on Tuesday to discuss the 1996 results and the latest version of the government's conditions on the privatisation.

The results of the profitable defence electronics group will be published on Wednesday and chairman Marcel Roulet is scheduled to give a news conference where he will be asked to comment on a series of rumours and newspaper reports.
Lagardere Groupe, winner of a previous aborted privatisation attempt, is a declared candidate, teamed up with British Aerospace Plc, with which it has the Matra-BAe Dynamics missiles joint-venture.
Alcatel Alsthom, which lost out in last year's proceedings, has teamed up with aerospace group Aerospatiale and fighter jet builder Dassault Aviation.

Le Monde said the government terms and conditions would elaborate on its desire to "assemble the biggest possible industrial capacity" in the defence sector and allow "joint bids with a group leader".
"The offer elaborated by Alcatel Alsthom, in association with Dassault and Aerospatiale, corresponds to this definition," the newspaper added.

Earlier on Tuesday, officials at Alcatel, Aerospatiale and Dassault had no comment on a report in the La Tribune newspaper detailing the capital structure of an enlarged Thomson-CSF if they won the state's 58 percent stake.
The paper did not indicate what the companies would pay for the stake but said that after a complex deal, Alcatel would own between 51 and 71 percent of Thomson-CSF.

A merged Aerospatiale-Dassault combination -- itself slated for privatisation -- would have seven to 10 percent, Dassault Industries 10 to 15 percent and Thomson-CSF staff five percent. A quarter of the shares would remain listed on the Paris stock exchange.
Alcatel would transfer around eight billion francs ($1.4 billion) worth of defence activities -- military telecoms and satellites -- to Thomson-CSF.

Aerospatiale, also the French partner in the Airbus Industrie civil plane consortium, would transfer its satellites activities -- estimated at five billion francs -- as well as its 34 percent stake in the Sextant Avionique joint venture to partner Thomson-CSF.
Dassault Industries, the holding company of the Dassault family which controls Dassault Electronique and has a 50 percent stake in Dassault Aviation, would put Dassault Electronique into Thomson-CSF.
The state owns much of the rest of Dassault Aviation.

La Tribune, putting a four billion franc value on the Dassault assets going to Thomson-CSF, did not make clear whether only the 58 percent or so of Dassault Electronique owned by Dassault Industrie was involved or the listed part as well.
Finally, La Tribune said Thomson-CSF's missiles activities, worth some four billion francs, could go to Aerospatiale.

When asked about the plan, Dassault chairman Serge Dassault and Aerospatiale chairman Yves Michot refused to comment on the La Tribune article at a news briefing of the GIFAS French aerospace industry association on Tuesday.
Last year, the government tried to privatise Thomson SA as a whole and in October said it preferred a joint bid by Lagardere and South Korea's Daewoo Electronics.
But it had to cancel the plan after the Privatisation Commission baulked at the terms of a deal to sell consumer electronics group Thomson Multimedia to Daewoo for one franc.
Thomson Multimedia, wholly owned by Thomson SA, will now be privatised seperately at a later date. ($ = 5.763 French Francs)
